title: Maha Shivaratri (the night vigil)
hook: a pillar of fire with no top and no bottom, a swan flying up, a boar digging down, and a flower that told a lie

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maha Shivaratri as it's kept: a fast, four watches, water poured, the mantra until dawn. Did you break something big into four? Today, back to the story many people say the night is for, and the part we skipped. Day one hundred forty-nine.

You heard this one on day ninety. Brahma and Vishnu arguing over who matters more, and a column of fire bursting up between them, with no top and no bottom. Vishnu became a boar and dug down. Brahma became a swan and flew up. Neither found an end, and Vishnu came back and said so. Tonight, on the great night itself, look again at two things we passed quickly. A small, sweet-smelling flower, drifting down out of the dark. And the pillar, which didn't stay in the story. People say it came down to earth in places you can still visit.
screen: `DAY NINETY: THE PILLAR WITH NO END.` → `A FLOWER DRIFTING DOWN.` → `A PILLAR YOU CAN VISIT.`

segments.voice: In the Shiva Purana's telling, the flower has a name: ketaki, the fragrant screwpine blossom. Brahma, worn out and empty-handed, meets it falling from somewhere far above him, and asks it a favor. Back me up. The flower agrees. So Brahma returns and says he reached the top, and the ketaki says yes, I saw him there. Then the pillar opens and Shiva steps out. Vishnu, who admitted his limit, is honored. Brahma is rebuked, and the story says that's why so few temples are built for him. And the flower gets its own sentence: it will never be offered in Shiva's worship. Many temples still leave it out. Notice who the story bothers to punish. Not only the one who lied, but the witness who said yes to something it never saw. Now the pillar. It's called the jyotirlinga: jyotis, light, and linga, a sign. And the tradition doesn't leave it in the sky. Hindus speak of twelve jyotirlinga shrines across India, places where Shiva is said to have shown himself as that light: Somnath on the Gujarat coast, Kashi Vishwanath in Varanasi, Kedarnath high in the Himalayas, Rameshwaram in the far south, and eight more. On Maha Shivaratri their lines run through the night. And in many South Indian Shiva temples, the scene is carved on the back wall of the shrine: Shiva in the pillar, a swan above, a boar below. This is a Shaiva story, told by Shiva's devotees; Vaishnava Hindus tell their own stories, where Vishnu is the source, and Hindus hold these side by side. Day ninety honored the one who said I don't know. Tonight honors its twin: don't vouch for what you didn't see.
screen: `THE KETAKI SAYS YES.` · `THE FALSE WITNESS IS BARRED.` · `JYOTIRLINGA: TWELVE SHRINES OF LIGHT.` · `CARVED ON THE BACK WALL.` · then, large: `DON'T VOUCH FOR WHAT YOU DIDN'T SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check your flowers. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days to something you passed on: a bit of news, a claim about someone, a story you repeated as if you'd seen it. Hold it up, gently, like the ketaki in Brahma's hand. Ask one question. Did I see this, or did I just say yes? No blame. Just sort it: seen, or heard. Then let the breath settle, and rest in what you actually know. The bell holds the time.
Maha Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, which many say remembers the pillar of light that had no end.
Your line: Maha Shivaratri, the night vigil. Today, before you vouch for anything, ask: did I see it? No flower, no bluff. Day one hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Many Hindus remember the Lingodbhava, Shiva appearing from an endless pillar of light, on Maha Shivaratri; temples often show it carved on the back wall of the shrine, devotees keep the night's vigil before the lingam, and the twelve jyotirlinga temples draw crowds through the night.

fork.setup: you're the ketaki flower, drifting down. Brahma asks you to say you saw him reach the top. what do you do?
fork.reveal: in the story the flower says yes, and that's why, people say, the ketaki is never offered to Shiva. the witness is held to account along with the liar.

original.note: Sanskrit: jyotis, light, and linga, sign or mark. the pillar of light.

trapdoor: what you thought: a contest between gods.
what it means: a story that honors the one who admitted his limit, and holds both the liar and the false witness to account.
what a scholar hears: Lingodbhava, told in the Shiva Purana and other Puranas, carved on the back wall of many South Indian Shiva shrines, and tied to the twelve jyotirlinga temples.

notes: Lingodbhava: Shiva Purana, Vidyeshvara Samhita chs. 5–9, and Linga Purana 1.17. Confirm refs.
